---
title: "Unit 2: Attributes, Joins, and Classification"
---

Geometry says where; attributes say what. This unit is about the tables behind every GIS layer and what you can do with them. It starts with attribute tables and SQL queries, then links tables to each other with keys and table joins, and links layers that share no key by their location, with spatial joins. It ends by turning a column of numbers into a map, choosing the classes for a choropleth map. By the end of the unit you can query, join, and map attribute data in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.

## Chapter 5: [Attribute Data and Queries](../chapters/attribute-queries.qmd)

Geometry says where; attributes say what. This chapter looks at the attribute table, its records and fields, the data types that store them and the binary limits behind them, and the levels of measurement that decide which questions make sense. It then teaches attribute queries in SQL, from simple comparisons to AND, OR, NOT, brackets, LIKE, BETWEEN, and IN, with a way to check any query using sets and Venn diagrams, and the trap of NULL values.

[Chapter 5 quiz](../chapters/attribute-queries-quiz.qmd)
:::

## Chapter 6: [Databases and Table Joins](../chapters/database-joins.qmd)

Most GIS data live in databases. This chapter explains what a database management system does, how relational databases link tables with primary and foreign keys, and how codes such as FIPS codes and GEOIDs serve as keys. It then teaches table joins: the destination and source tables, inner, left, right, and full joins, and how cardinality decides what a join can do, with ways to handle one-to-many relationships. It ends with a census join in QGIS, and the problems that most often break a join.

[Chapter 6 quiz](../chapters/database-joins-quiz.qmd)

## Chapter 7: [Spatial Joins](../chapters/spatial-joins.qmd)

When two layers share no key, location can link them. This chapter explains spatial predicates such as intersects, within, and contains, and the four kinds of spatial join, from simple inside joins to summarized distance joins. Worked examples match North Carolina towns to their nearest airports and septic systems to the geology beneath them. It covers cardinality, why distances need a projected coordinate system, six questions to plan any spatial join, and the tools that do the work in QGIS and ArcGIS Pro.

[Chapter 7 quiz](../chapters/spatial-joins-quiz.qmd)
:::

## Chapter 8: [Data Classing and Choropleth Maps](../chapters/data-classing.qmd)

The same data can tell different stories depending on how they are grouped into classes. This chapter explains why choropleth maps should show rates and densities rather than counts, how to choose the number of classes, and how the main classification methods work: equal interval, quantile, natural breaks (Jenks), arithmetic and geometric intervals, and standard deviation. Using the population density of North Carolina's 100 counties, it compares the methods with histograms and the goodness of variance fit.
